title: The Moving Sands: Frank Herbert, the Newsroom Years, and the Law Against Thinking Machines
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Puget Sound and the Burley Colony

stops.name: Tacoma, birth on the eighth of October
stops.date_confidence: attested; sources disagree on the full given names, one rendering him Franklin Patrick Herbert Jr. son of Frank Herbert Sr., another Frank Patrick Herbert Jr. son of Franklin Patrick Herbert Sr.
stops.campa: Franklin Patrick Herbert Jr. is born in Tacoma to Frank Herbert Sr. and Eileen McCarthy Herbert, in a city of timber wharves, smelter smoke, and the cold water of Puget Sound. His father's people had crossed to the county fifteen years before for a cooperative colony at Burley, on the far shore. Over the waterfront stands the ASARCO copper smelter, its stack five hundred and seventy-one feet of brick, throwing a plume out across the sound. It runs day and night through the whole of his childhood.
suggested_refs: Brian Herbert, Dreamer of Dune (2003), the family account of the Tacoma years

stops.name: Tacoma, the aunts and the vocation
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed; the maternal aunts' role in his upbringing and their hopes for a priestly vocation are reported in the family biography without dates, and the year here simply places the claim inside his Tacoma boyhood
stops.campa: His mother's family are the McCarthys, Irish Catholics in numbers, and it is her sisters rather than his parents who take charge of a good deal of his childhood. Several of them mean the boy for the priesthood and say so, and they say it early enough that he grows up knowing what he is intended for. He is instructed, taken to Mass, watched for signs of a calling. No seminary follows. The family biography records the aunts' hope without dates, and does not record what the boy ever said back to them.
suggested_refs: Brian Herbert, Dreamer of Dune (2003), on the McCarthy aunts and the intended priesthood

stops.name: Burley, the colony summers on the Kitsap side
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed; the Kitsap and Olympic peninsula boyhood is attested in O'Reilly and in the family biography, but only to the 1920s and 1930s at large, with no year and no parcel documented
stops.campa: Across the water in Kitsap County lies Burley, where his father's parents joined a cooperative colony in 1905. He spends stretches of boyhood on the Kitsap and Olympic peninsulas in the care of relatives, learning to hunt, to fish, and to handle a boat on tidal water. Thirty years later he will give the Fremen a discipline built entirely on the absence of water, and he will build it out of this country. Rain comes off the Pacific over the Olympic range and falls here in some of the heaviest quantities measured in the United States.
suggested_refs: Burley Colony, Kitsap County, the cooperative settlement his paternal grandparents joined in 1905

stops.name: Salem, the door of the Rowntree house
stops.date_confidence: attested year, month and day not recorded
stops.campa: At about eighteen he leaves Tacoma for good and turns up in Salem at the house of his aunt Peggy Rowntree, called Violet. Salem gives him a bed and a school year left to finish, and an aunt willing to keep somebody else's child through it. He enrolls in the town high school and stays until he has the diploma in hand. His parents are still living and he has left them behind; the sources record the flight and not its cause. What he was running from he never sets out in print, and no letter or interview reachable now answers the question on his behalf.
suggested_refs: The Rowntree household in Salem, Oregon, refuge of the 1938 flight from Tacoma

stops.name: Salem High School, the diploma
stops.date_confidence: attested year; the graduation month is inferred from the ordinary school calendar. The school was named Salem High School in 1938 and 1939 and was renamed North Salem only in 1954
stops.campa: He graduates from Salem High School on its Fourteenth Street campus, at eighteen, a year after arriving in the town. The building will be renamed North Salem fifteen years later, after the town grows a second high school. The diploma is the only formal credential he ever holds. He will enroll at a university later and lecture at one later still, and take a degree from neither. Everything he learns after June 1939 he gets out of newsrooms, out of public libraries, and out of the people he corners for an hour.
suggested_refs: North Salem High School, 765 14th Street NE, Salem, on the campus occupied since 1937

stops.name: Glendale, the age he lies about
stops.date_confidence: the year is attested; whether the Glendale job came before or after the June diploma is not settled by the sources, one placing it about 1938 to 1939 and another squarely in 1939, and the month here is a placement after graduation
stops.campa: He presents himself at the Glendale Star as a man old enough for the job and is hired. He is eighteen and has said otherwise. Nobody at the Star checks his age, then or afterwards. The paper puts him to the trade he will practise for the next thirty-three years: copy, photographs, deadlines, the daily obligation to make a stranger's business clear to another stranger who is in a hurry. He writes fiction on the nights of those same thirty-three years, and sells none of it until 1952.
suggested_refs: The Glendale Star, first masthead of a thirty-three-year newspaper career

stops.name: Salem, the Oregon Statesman
stops.date_confidence: attested year, month and day not recorded
stops.campa: Within the year he is back in Salem on the Oregon Statesman, working as photographer and in several other roles, in the town where his aunt took him in. The pattern that will hold until the last day of 1972 is already set: a newsroom for the money, a typewriter after hours for the other thing. The copy and the photographs sell week after week under the paper's masthead rather than his name. He is twenty years old and has worked at three papers already.
suggested_refs: The Oregon Statesman, Salem, where he worked as photographer and copy writer

stops.name: San Pedro, the first marriage
stops.date_confidence: attested year, month and day not recorded
stops.campa: In San Pedro, on the harbor south of Los Angeles, he marries Flora Lillian Parkinson. He is twenty years old and has been working newspapers for two of them. Of his three marriages this is the one that leaves least behind it: the record gives no address for the wedding and no cause for its end, and no letter from either of them survives anywhere it can be read. A daughter, Penelope, is born on the sixteenth of February 1942, and he will know her from a distance for the rest of his life. By 1943 the marriage is over.
suggested_refs: The 1941 San Pedro marriage record of Franklin P. Herbert and Flora L. Parkinson

stops.name: Port Hueneme, six months in the Seabees
stops.date_confidence: the year and the roughly six months of service are attested; no accessible source names his duty station, and the coordinate marks the Seabee advance base depot at Port Hueneme rather than a camp he is known to have occupied
stops.campa: He enlists in the Navy Seabees and serves roughly six months as a photographer before a head injury ends it and the Navy discharges him on medical grounds. The construction battalions bound for the Pacific stage through the advance base depot at Port Hueneme, a camp of graders and pontoon sections and men learning to lay an airstrip under fire. He leaves with a camera trade and a damaged head. Which station he actually served at, no accessible record names.
suggested_refs: Camp Rousseau, Port Hueneme, California, the Seabee advance base depot for the Pacific

stops.name: Portland, the Oregon Journal
stops.date_confidence: the Oregon Journal employment is attested but undated in accessible sources; the year here is a placement after the 1942 discharge and before the 1946 Seattle marriage
stops.campa: After the discharge he reports for the Oregon Journal in Portland, one more newsroom in a decade of them. He is twenty-three, divorced, and the father at a distance of a girl he will know mostly by letter. Everything he has published so far has gone out under somebody else's headline, on somebody else's deadline, in type nobody keeps. The first magazine to print his name over a story is nine years off. He writes fiction at night and it comes back.
suggested_refs: The Oregon Journal, Portland, one of the postwar newsroom jobs of the rejection years

stops.name: University of Washington, the writing class
stops.date_confidence: attested year, month and day not recorded
stops.campa: He enrolls at the University of Washington on a campus filling with men back from the war, and takes a creative writing class. Beverly Ann Stuart is in it, and she has already sold a story to Modern Romance, which is one more than he has sold anywhere. Twenty-four years later this same university will hire him to lecture in general and interdisciplinary studies, an arrangement that asks for no diploma and gets none. Of the class itself nothing survives in any reachable source but the fact that the two of them sat in one room for a term. He does not finish the degree.
suggested_refs: The University of Washington creative writing course of 1946, where Herbert met Beverly Ann Stuart

stops.name: Seattle, the marriage to Beverly Ann Stuart
stops.date_confidence: the 1946 Seattle marriage is attested; the twentieth of June is reconstructed and is not confirmed in any accessible source
stops.campa: He marries Beverly Ann Stuart in Seattle. She is a writer in her own right and puts her own work down to take the advertising jobs that keep a household running while her husband writes at night and collects rejections. The family will move when the papers move: Seattle, Sonoma County, San Francisco, Marin, back north. Every manuscript he finishes goes under her pencil before it goes to an editor. The marriage lasts thirty-eight years and ends with her death.
suggested_refs: Beverly Ann Stuart Herbert, first reader and editor of every Herbert manuscript from 1946 to 1984

stops.name: Seattle, Brian born into the rejection years
stops.date_confidence: Brian Herbert's birth in 1947 is attested; accessible sources do not name the city, and the coordinate follows the household's documented Seattle residence of 1946
stops.campa: Brian is born in 1947 into a household run on one wage and one typewriter. Beverly sets her own fiction aside and takes the advertising work, and the money that carries the family through the next eighteen years is hers. Fifty-five years on, this boy will publish the war his father declined to describe. For now his father files copy by day and writes at night, and every manuscript goes under Beverly's pencil before it goes out, and comes back from the editors anyway, with a printed slip in the envelope.
suggested_refs: Brian Herbert, later co-author of the Dune prequels, born 1947

stops.name: Santa Rosa, the Press-Democrat and the first sale
stops.date_confidence: O'Reilly dates the California move and the Press-Democrat job to April 1949 and Wikipedia to 1949; one chronology source carries 1950, and that year is rejected here as an error of one
stops.campa: The family moves to California and Herbert takes a desk at the Santa Rosa Press-Democrat, in a Sonoma County town of orchards, canneries, and one hotel big enough to hold a convention. He files local copy and shoots local pictures for the daily. He is twenty-nine and the author of nothing anyone has heard of. Bruce Calvin is born in 1951. In April 1952 Startling Stories prints Looking for Something, the first science fiction he ever sells. The working week does not change by an hour on account of it.
suggested_refs: Startling Stories, April 1952, 'Looking for Something', his first science fiction publication

stops.name: Washington, the Library of Congress desk
stops.date_confidence: O'Reilly dates the Washington work to 1954 and places it at the Library of Congress; one chronology source gives 1952 and one geography source 1956, and 1956 is impossible because Cordon left the Senate on 3 January 1955. Month and day not recorded
stops.campa: He takes a season away from newspapers to work in Washington as a campaign hand and speechwriter for Guy Cordon, Republican senator from Oregon, and as a research assistant based at the Library of Congress. The job is to draft another man's convictions and hand them over to be spoken in that man's voice, by hands whose names appear nowhere on the paper. Cordon's service in the Senate ends on the third of January 1955, and the work ends with it. Herbert goes back to the coast and back to a newsroom.
suggested_refs: Guy Cordon, United States senator from Oregon, 4 March 1944 to 3 January 1955

segments.name: The Sand That Would Not Stop

stops.name: San Francisco, Under Pressure in Astounding
stops.date_confidence: the November 1955 serialization is attested; his residence and employer in that year are not established, since Wikipedia gives about a decade at the San Francisco Examiner without start year and O'Reilly puts him there only from 1959, and the coordinate is a Bay Area placement rather than a documented address
stops.campa: Astounding Science Fiction begins running Under Pressure in November, a serial about the crew of a submarine tug hauling stolen oil out of enemy water, and about the crewman among them who is going insane, and about which of the others can tell. It appears as a book the following year under the title The Dragon in the Sea. His first novel is a study of a closed system with four men inside it and no way out but through. Where he was living that winter, and which paper paid him, the sources do not agree.
suggested_refs: Under Pressure, serialized in Astounding Science Fiction from November 1955; book form as The Dragon in the Sea (1956)

stops.name: Florence, the poverty grass on the moving dunes
stops.date_confidence: attested year, month and day not recorded
stops.campa: On the coast near Florence the Department of Agriculture has been planting European beach grass to hold dunes that bury roads, lakes, and standing timber as they travel. Herbert comes as a journalist to write up the program and stays with it long past the length of an article. The article he never finishes; it reaches print only in 2005, nineteen years after his death. What he takes away instead is sand understood as a thing that moves and has an appetite. He hires a light plane and goes up to see the whole field of it at once.
stops.quote: could swallow whole cities, lakes, rivers, highways
stops.quote_source: Frank Herbert to his literary agent on the Oregon dunes, 1957, quoted in Wikipedia, 'Dune (novel)'
suggested_refs: They Stopped the Moving Sands, the unfinished 1957 article, printed in The Road to Dune (2005)

stops.name: La Push, the sentence about eating the earth
stops.date_confidence: the wording of the remark is attested; its speaker and date are not settled between sources, one giving Howard Hansen, raised on the Quileute reservation, speaking in 1958, another an unnamed Hoh man on the Olympic coast in the 1930s. That the exchange happened on this ground is reconstructed in either version
stops.campa: Howard Hansen grew up on the Quileute reservation at the mouth of the Quillayute river, where the surf runs in past James Island, and he has a long argument with Herbert about what is being done to land. He puts it in one sentence about white men, the earth, and North Africa. Herbert still has the Florence dunes in his notebooks, and within a year he has begun the reading that produces Arrakis. One account gives the sentence to Hansen here in 1958. Another gives it to an unnamed Hoh man on this same coast in the 1930s. Was it carried from boyhood, or heard at thirty-eight?
stops.quote: White men are eating the earth. They're gonna turn this whole planet into a wasteland, just like North Africa.
stops.quote_source: Howard Hansen to Frank Herbert, 1958, cited in Wikipedia, 'Dune (novel)'
suggested_refs: Daniel Immerwahr on the 1958 remark as an origin of Arrakis

stops.name: San Francisco, the Examiner and California Living
stops.date_confidence: O'Reilly places him at the San Francisco Examiner from 1959, for over ten years, mostly on California Living; Wikipedia gives about a decade without a start year. The coordinate is near the Examiner building at 110 Fifth Street
stops.campa: He joins the San Francisco Examiner and settles into California Living, its Sunday supplement, where he will write and edit for the better part of ten years. The building stands south of Market Street; the trade is the one he has practised since he was eighteen. The supplement pays for a house and asks nothing of his nights. In the same year he begins the reading for a novel about a desert planet. The two occupations run side by side for the next six years.
suggested_refs: California Living, the Sunday supplement of the San Francisco Examiner, which Herbert wrote and edited

stops.name: Fairfax, the six years of reading
stops.date_confidence: the 1959 start of the Dune research is attested; the Marin County residence is reconstructed and not confirmed against a primary source, and the month is a placement inside the year
stops.campa: The household is living in Marin County, north of the Golden Gate, when the research closes over him and does not let go for six years. He reads desert ecology and Bedouin water discipline. He reads the life of Muhammad, who came out of dry country with a book and an army behind him, and Moses leading a people forty years through wilderness toward a land they had been promised. He reads on drugs, on prophecy, on the politics of a single scarce commodity. Beverly's advertising wage carries the household through all six years.
stops.quote: highly organized research is guaranteed to produce nothing new
stops.quote_source: Dune (1965), Appendix I, on the method of the planetologist Pardot Kynes
suggested_refs: Herbert's Dune research files, 1959 to 1965, on ecology, Islamic history, prophecy, and psychology

stops.name: San Francisco, Dune World begins in Analog
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Analog starts running Dune World in December, three installments under John W. Campbell, and follows it in January 1965 with The Prophet of Dune in five more. Readers meet the Bene Gesserit, whose sisters carry inside them the memory of every woman in their line: Jung's collective unconscious given a bloodline, a breeding program, and a political office. For two years the magazine is the only form the book has, because no house will print it whole. The letters arrive at Campbell's desk in volume, for and against, month after month.
stops.quote: I must not fear. Fear is the mind-killer. Fear is the little-death that brings total obliteration. I will face my fear. I will permit it to pass over me and through me.
stops.quote_source: Dune (1965), the Bene Gesserit Litany Against Fear
suggested_refs: Analog Science Fact and Fiction: 'Dune World', December 1963 to February 1964; 'The Prophet of Dune', January to May 1965

stops.name: San Francisco, twenty rejections and a manual publisher
stops.date_confidence: the August 1965 publication and the 7,500 dollar advance are attested and the count of rejections is given as more than twenty without a figure; one account of the first edition gives October rather than August, and the discrepancy is not resolved here
stops.campa: More than twenty publishers turn Dune down. It is too long, too slow, too strange, and the science fiction houses know their market. The book is bought at last by Chilton, of Philadelphia, whose business is automobile repair manuals, for seven thousand five hundred dollars against royalties. No source places Herbert in Philadelphia at any point in the transaction. It goes on sale at five dollars ninety-five, sells badly, and is reviewed as something not quite of its field.
suggested_refs: Chilton Book Company, Philadelphia, publisher of the first edition of Dune, August 1965

stops.name: San Francisco, the commandment in the appendix
stops.date_confidence: the content is attested across the published novel and its terminology appendix; the date is a placement immediately after publication, since no composition date exists for the appendix material
stops.campa: The book carries in its epigraphs and its terminology a war it never shows. Some ten thousand years before Paul Atreides is born, the thinking machines were destroyed in the Butlerian Jihad, and the Orange Catholic Bible was assembled out of the faiths that survived, carrying one commandment over the rest. After it, computation is a crime and the work falls back on people: Mentats trained as living calculators, Bene Gesserit adepts drilled in observation and control of the body, Guild Navigators warped by spice into seeing a course through folded space. The war itself is never given a scene in any of the six novels he writes.
stops.quote: Thou shalt not make a machine in the likeness of a human mind.
stops.quote_source: The Orange Catholic Bible, quoted in Dune (1965); the wording is uniform across secondary sources, and one lens of this research could not reach a primary page carrying it
suggested_refs: Dune (1965), Appendix and Terminology of the Imperium, on the Butlerian Jihad and its prohibition

stops.name: San Francisco, the Nebula and the Hugo
stops.date_confidence: the two awards are attested, the Nebula banquet to March 1966 in New York and the Hugo to Tricon in Cleveland, 1 to 5 September 1966; no source places Herbert at either ceremony, and the coordinate stays where he was living and working
stops.campa: Dune takes the first Nebula Award for Best Novel ever given, and the next year ties the Hugo with Roger Zelazny's novel, serialized as ...And Call Me Conrad and published as This Immortal. It is the first tie in the Best Novel category. The book more than twenty houses turned down has taken both prizes the field possesses, one of them in the year it was invented. Sales will eventually reach close to twenty million copies in dozens of languages, and have not begun to. Herbert is forty-five and still filing supplement copy for the Examiner on a weekly schedule.
stops.quote: Once men turned their thinking over to machines in the hope that this would set them free. But that only permitted other men with machines to enslave them.
stops.quote_source: Dune (1965), Bene Gesserit teaching, attributed to Reverend Mother Gaius Helen Mohiam
suggested_refs: The inaugural Nebula Award for Best Novel; Tricon, the 24th World Science Fiction Convention, Cleveland, September 1966

stops.name: Seattle, the Post-Intelligencer and Dune Messiah
stops.date_confidence: attested year, month and day not recorded. An entry in one lens placed the writing of Dune Messiah at Port Townsend, which is wrong for 1969: the Olympic Peninsula property dates from the 1970s and he was at the Examiner until this year
stops.campa: He is back in Seattle writing about education for the Post-Intelligencer, and publishes Dune Messiah, in which the messiah of the first book is shown for a disaster: a man whose holy war has killed billions in his name, who walks blind into the desert at the end of it. Paul commands human minds because the other kind was outlawed millennia before he was born. Readers who wanted more of the hero are furious and stay furious for years. He tells interviewer after interviewer that this is the book he set out to write from the beginning.
suggested_refs: Dune Messiah (1969), the sequel written to invert the messiah of the first book

stops.name: University of Washington, the lecturer without a degree
stops.date_confidence: attested year, month and day not recorded
stops.campa: The university that never gave him a degree hires him to lecture in general and interdisciplinary studies, the one department shaped to fit a man who reads ecology, psychology, Islamic history and desert hydrology as a single subject. He teaches on the strength of a novel, in the buildings where he sat as a student twenty-four years earlier and left without finishing. Two miles off, the Post-Intelligencer still wants education copy from him every week. Four of the six Dune books are not yet written and he is fifty years old.
stops.quote: A process cannot be understood by stopping it. Understanding must move with the flow of the process, must join it and flow with it.
stops.quote_source: Dune (1965), given as the First Law of Mentat
suggested_refs: Herbert's appointment as lecturer in general and interdisciplinary studies, University of Washington, 1970

stops.name: Saigon, the ecological consultant
stops.date_confidence: the year and the consulting role are attested; the source names Vietnam without a city or province, and the coordinate is a country-level placement
stops.campa: He works in Vietnam as a social and ecological consultant, in a country being stripped of its forest cover by the ton while he is inside it. He arrives as a paid observer rather than as a novelist, and nobody there has read him. The argument at the centre of Dune, that an ecology can be wrecked faster than anyone learns to read it, is not a metaphor in Vietnam in 1972; it is the water table and the canopy. What he wrote for whoever hired him has not surfaced, and no source names the province he worked in.
stops.quote: Survival is the ability to swim in strange water.
stops.quote_source: Dune (1965), given as a Bene Gesserit proverb
suggested_refs: Herbert's 1972 consulting work in Vietnam as a social and ecological adviser

stops.name: Pakistan, the arid country and the last deadline
stops.date_confidence: the year and the consulting role are attested; no Pakistani city is named in any accessible source and the coordinate defaults to Islamabad, and the month is a placement inside the consulting season
stops.campa: The same consulting season takes him to Pakistan: dry country with mountains at its back, water argued over village by village, an irrigation politics old enough to have outlived several empires and to have been rebuilt by each of them. Arrakis has been in print for seven years and he is walking a real arid landscape as a man paid for his judgment about how people live on it. At the end of the year he quits newspaper work for good, thirty-three years after the Glendale Star hired an eighteen-year-old who said he was older.
suggested_refs: Herbert's 1972 consulting work in Pakistan; he left newspaper writing at the end of that year

stops.name: Port Townsend, the demonstration project
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed; the Olympic Peninsula property is documented in general biographical accounts as an ecological demonstration project, without a street address or firm dates, and the coordinate marks the town centre
stops.campa: On the Olympic Peninsula he builds what he calls an ecological demonstration project: solar collectors, a wind plant, methane drawn off chicken droppings, a garden meant to feed the household that tends it. He is testing at the scale of one family the proposition his fiction argues at the scale of a planet, that a place and the people on it are one machine with no spare parts. This is the peninsula where he learned as a boy to handle a boat. He keeps accounts of every gallon of water the property uses, in the wettest country in the United States.
stops.quote: From water does all life begin.
stops.quote_source: Dune (1965), a Fremen saying, tied in the text to the Shah-Nama
suggested_refs: The Herberts' solar and wind powered property on the Olympic Peninsula, called Xanadu
sources: general biographical accounts of the property, parcel unverified

stops.name: Kailua, the second house
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed; sources place a Hawaiian home from the early 1970s without naming island or town, Kailua on Oahu is commonly cited but not independently sourced, and other accounts say Maui or Kauai. The coordinate is the commonly cited one and should be treated as unfixed
stops.campa: From the early 1970s the household keeps a second home in Hawaii and the year divides between one Pacific coast and another. In 1974 Beverly begins treatment for lung cancer, and the two houses become a rotation organised partly around a climate that suits her. He writes the sequels in both places and dates none of the drafts by address. Which island the second house stood on the sources do not agree about: Oahu is the name given most often, Maui and Kauai also appear, and none of the three is documented.
suggested_refs: The Hawaiian residence of the Herbert household from the early 1970s, island unconfirmed

stops.name: Port Townsend, Children of Dune
stops.date_confidence: the 1976 publication is attested; that the book was finished at the Olympic Peninsula house is reconstruction, since no source names the desk it was written at
stops.campa: Children of Dune appears and does what neither of its predecessors managed, becoming a genuine hardcover bestseller. It is the third book and the first that makes him rich. The Fremen theocracy in it runs on prescience and breeding programs and trained memory, because after the Jihad there is nothing else it can run on: no computer anywhere in the Imperium, ten thousand years after the last one was smashed. The twins at the centre of it inherit the memories of everyone who came before them.
suggested_refs: Children of Dune (1976), the first Dune novel to reach the hardcover bestseller lists

stops.name: Port Townsend, God Emperor and the fullest gloss
stops.date_confidence: the 1981 publication is attested; the Olympic Peninsula location is reconstruction, and the month is not recorded
stops.campa: God Emperor of Dune is published: three and a half millennia after the first book, a man who has let himself become a sandworm rules the galaxy in order to teach humanity, by tyranny and by boredom, never to follow anybody anywhere again. In it Leto II gives the fullest account Herbert ever writes in his own hand of what the Butlerian Jihad was, calling it a semi-religious social upheaval, born of human disgust at how thoroughly the machines had come to guide them. That gloss is the whole of it. It runs to a few lines, and names no battle and no date.
suggested_refs: God Emperor of Dune (1981), Leto II on the Butlerian Jihad as a semi-religious social upheaval
sources: Frank Herbert, God Emperor of Dune (1981)

stops.name: Port Townsend, the death of Beverly Herbert
stops.date_confidence: the date and the long lung cancer illness are attested; no consulted source names her place of death, and the coordinate defaults to the couple's Olympic Peninsula property rather than the Hawaiian house
stops.campa: Beverly Ann Herbert dies of the lung cancer she has been treated for since 1974, in the thirty-eighth year of the marriage. She had set down her own writing early to earn the money the household lived on, and had edited every book her husband published, first reader and last check on all of it. Thirty-eight years of manuscripts went across her desk before they went to New York, from the ones nobody bought to the ones that sold twenty million. No consulted source names the place of her death; one account puts it on the peninsula, another in Hawaii.
suggested_refs: Beverly Ann Herbert, died 7 February 1984, place of death unrecorded in consulted sources

stops.name: Port Townsend, Heretics of Dune and the Lynch film
stops.date_confidence: the 1984 publication and the 1984 release of David Lynch's film are attested; the month here is a placement inside the year and the writing location is reconstruction
stops.campa: Heretics of Dune appears in the year his wife dies. The novel runs fifteen centuries past the God Emperor and finds the law still holding: the Bene Tleilax growing people in tanks, the Sisterhood breeding and drilling its own, the Honored Matres returning out of the Scattering with a weapon made of trained bodies. Nobody in it builds a computer, and no government in it is enforcing the prohibition that stops them. In December, David Lynch's film of the first book opens in American theatres.
suggested_refs: Heretics of Dune (1984); Dune, directed by David Lynch (1984)

stops.name: Port Townsend, the third marriage and the sixth book
stops.date_confidence: the 1985 marriage and the 1985 publication are attested; no source names the ceremony's location, and the coordinate defaults to the Olympic Peninsula property
stops.campa: A year after Beverly's death he marries Theresa Diane Shackelford. Chapterhouse: Dune appears the same year, the sixth novel and the last he writes, closing the saga still bound by the law the Orange Catholic Bible laid down after the Jihad, and ending on a scene that opens rather than shuts: two figures in a no-ship out past everything charted, watched by powers the book declines to name. There are notes toward a seventh book in the house, and an outline of about thirty pages. He is sixty-four.
stops.quote: Since every individual is accountable ultimately to the self, the formation of that self demands our utmost care and attention.
suggested_refs: Chapterhouse: Dune (1985), the last novel of the original six

stops.name: Madison, the University of Wisconsin Hospital
stops.date_confidence: the date, the city, and the cause of death are attested; the specific hospital is an inference from the fact that the University of Wisconsin Hospital is Madison's major surgical centre, not a named source
stops.campa: He is in Madison, Wisconsin, recovering from surgery for pancreatic cancer, when a massive pulmonary embolism kills him on the eleventh of February, at sixty-five. It is two years after Beverly, twenty-one years after Dune, a few months after the last of the six books, one year into a third marriage. He had lived his whole life within reach of salt water, on Puget Sound, in San Francisco, on the Olympic Peninsula, in Hawaii. Madison is more than a thousand miles inland.
suggested_refs: The University of Wisconsin Hospital, Madison, the city of record for Herbert's death

stops.name: Madison, the house of his son Bruce
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed; sources say only that he died while recovering from surgery, and whether the embolism took him in the hospital or at his son's house is unresolved between accounts. The date is set a day after the death to keep the two accounts distinct on the map
stops.campa: Bruce Calvin Herbert, the second son, born in 1951, keeps a house in Madison, and his father is staying there through the recovery. Whether the embolism took him in a hospital room or in that house the record does not settle; the accounts have never been reconciled. What became of Frank Herbert's remains after February 1986 no reachable source states, and no burial or cremation record was located for him anywhere. Bruce dies of an AIDS-related pneumonia in 1993, at forty-two, seven years after his father.

stops.name: Fullerton, the papers in the Pollak Library
stops.date_confidence: the archive holding is attested; no accessible source gives an accession date, and the date shown is a placement after his death
stops.campa: The Frank Herbert papers, draft manuscripts of Dune among them, come to rest in University Archives and Special Collections at the Pollak Library, California State University, Fullerton, inside the science fiction collection assembled by Willis McNelly. Fullerton is a flat Orange County campus with no other claim on him: no dune, no rain forest, no newsroom he ever worked in. The drafts of a book about a planet without water sit in boxes there under air conditioning. Sixteen years later his son says a thirty-page outline for a seventh book was found among them. Whose war the trilogy written from it is, no consulted source settles.
suggested_refs: Frank Herbert papers, Willis McNelly Science Fiction Collection, Pollak Library, CSU Fullerton

stops.name: Seattle Center, the Hall of Fame at twenty years
stops.date_confidence: attested year, month and day not recorded
stops.campa: Twenty years after his death Herbert is inducted into the Science Fiction Hall of Fame, by then housed at the Science Fiction Museum at Seattle Center, thirty miles up the sound from the Tacoma he was born in and two miles from the newsroom where he wrote about schools. The Hall was founded in another state entirely and moved west a few years before the ceremony, so that a man who spent his life on this water is enrolled at home by an accident of real estate. He is enrolled posthumously.

stops.name: Point Defiance, Dune Peninsula on the poisoned ground
stops.date_confidence: attested month and year, day not recorded
stops.campa: Metro Parks Tacoma opens Dune Peninsula and the Frank Herbert Trail at Point Defiance, on the water where the ASARCO copper smelter stood for a century, its stack visible from every hill in the city of his childhood. Before the park could open the ground had to be capped with clean soil laid over arsenic and slag, under a federal cleanup order. The city that made him gives his name to the piece of itself it had to detoxify first. The paths run out over the capped shoreline, and the sound is on three sides of them.
suggested_refs: Dune Peninsula and the Frank Herbert Trail, Point Defiance Park, Tacoma, opened July 2019 on the former ASARCO Superfund site
